newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: Taleban cancel Afghan New Year celebrations.
newsitem.headline: Taleban cancel Afghan New Year celebrations.

text.p: The Islamic Taleban militia has cancelled the Afghan New Year's day public holiday, which falls on Friday, and banned all New Year festivities, saying celebrations of any kind are against Islamic Sharia law.
The ban on Nowruz (New Year's day) celebrations is the latest in a stream of Taleban edicts designed to enforce the purist movement's strict interpretation of Islam throughout Afghanistan.

"As all days are the same and there is no difference between the first and the last day of the month, and also because Nowruz day (New Year's day) has no particular significance except celebration, Nawruz has been prohibited according to Sharia law," the Taleban Supreme Court in Kabul said in a statement broadcast on Taleban-controlled radio on Wednesday night.
"Therefore, organising special ceremonies on this day, picnics, arranging special food or declaring the first day of the New Year a public holiday are against Sharia rulings."
Nowruz is widely celebrated in Afghanistan, Iran, Central Asia and Kurdish areas of Turkey, Iraq and Syria.
In Afghanistan it is also known as Farmers' Day, and in the past has been marked by fairs exhibiting prize animals and farm produce in provincial centres and in the Kabul district of Khair Khana.

Pilgrims traditionally flock to the shrine of Hazrat Ali, cousin and son-in-law of the Prophet Mohammed, in the northern city of Mazar-i-Sharif on March 21. A religious banner is raised to announce the beginning of spring and coming of the New Year.

This is the time of the Guli Surkh, or Red Blossom-Tulip, Festival, symbolising hopes for prosperity. Apart from fairs, Afghans mark the occasion with games of buzkashi, in which teams of horsemen fight for the carcass of a headless goat.
